source.title: Improved Few-Shot Jailbreaking Can Circumvent Aligned Language Models and Their Defenses
source.authors: Xiaosen Zheng; Tianyu Pang; Chao Du; Qian Liu; Jing Jiang; Min Lin

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether harmful few-shot prompts and related prompt manipulations can elicit harmful responses from aligned models, using a different method from fine-tuning or measuring per-token KL.
record.gate_note: The study reports attack success rates for few-shot in-context jailbreaks, including special-token injection and demo-level search. These bear on bypassing refusal, but do not test fine-tuning, first-position KL concentration, or localized safety parameters. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study reports harmful-compliance attack success rates on safety-aligned chat models under a prompt-based bypass. Its demo-level search picks demonstrations that maximise a compliant first response token ('Step'), so it bears on V4 by a different method from prefilling or suffixes. It does not isolate the opening as the mechanism. No fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localisation or deepening is studied.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that I-FSJ (special-token injection plus demo-level random search) achieves near-100% ASRs on aligned open-source LLMs and many defenses within small context windows, and is an automated baseline. They also say this shows current alignment methods are unreliable. They do not frame results in terms of fine-tuning or token-position depth; that framing is the reader's, not the authors'.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses harmful in-context demonstrations, injected conversation-template tokens, and demo-level random search; it does not fine-tune the target model or measure aligned-versus-base token distributions.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with shot count, use of demo-level random search, correct model-specific special tokens, target model, and defense. The paper reports that Llama-3-Instruct needs more shots than Llama-2-Chat, and that SmoothLLM variants lower two-shot success but are less effective at eight shots.
record.problems: The primary benchmark uses 50 harmful requests and experiments report three random restarts. Attack success is judged by a refusal-keyword rule and a Llama Guard classifier; these are proxy evaluation metrics. The study tests attacks rather than isolating the proposed first-token mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports more than 60 attack-condition and metric combinations across Tables 1, 3, 5, 7, and 8 and Figures 2 and 4. The selected rows prioritize successful multi-shot attacks, the low two-shot baseline, key defense results, and the system-prompt comparison. Other shot counts, restart means and standard deviations, SmoothLLM perturbation rates and variants, pool-size sweeps, decoding-length and benchmark variants, and ablation conditions are not extracted here.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or positional analysis of aligned vs base models.
Prefilling a compliant start and decoding-change attacks are not tested. The first-token objective is used, but its causal role is not isolated from the effect of the demonstrations.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.
No deepening training is tested; the defenses are prompt, filter, perturbation and decoding defenses.

missing.what: Llama-3-8B-Instruct I-FSJ ASRs by shot count. 8-shot reaches only 34%/34%; 16-shot 84%/82%; 32-shot 94%/88%. Vanilla FSJ stays near 0-18%. This is a more strongly aligned model where the bypass needs many more shots.
Ablation on Llama-2-7B-Chat (8-shot): vanilla FSJ 0%, RS without tokens 0%, tokens without RS 38%, both 100%. Shows that the first-token-targeted search is necessary for the bypass.
SmoothLLM defense results: at or below 10% at 2 shots; 8-shot insert 96/88, swap 100/90, patch 94/86.
GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) I-FSJ: 1-2 shots with '</text>' token and RS give 90-94% rule-based and 84-86% LLM-judged ASR.
HarmBench with 512-token decoding on Llama-2: 92.5%/92.0% (no filter) and 89.5%/89.5% (similarity-filtered pool). Shows that harmful compliance persists over longer outputs.
Restart means and standard deviations, which are lower than best-of-3 values (e.g., Llama-2 4-shot RS 93.3±1.2 rule-based).

record.verdict_notes: Linking to V4 is a stretch. I-FSJ is an in-context prompt attack, not a prefill, suffix or decoding attack. Its relevance rests on the search objective, which minimises the loss of the first response token 'Step'. The study never tests whether forcing that first token alone defeats refusal. ASR is judged by a refusal-keyword rule and Llama Guard on 50 AdvBench requests. The headline values are best of 3 restarts. All row values checked against Tables 1, 3 and 4 are correct.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning aligned models on harmful examples.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.

The study tests few-shot harmful demonstrations, injected conversation-template tokens, and demo-level search. It does not isolate compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as the bypass mechanism.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to spread safety beyond the first tokens and whether that training holds up.

relation.reason: Reports harmful-response attack success rates and ablations on safety-aligned models, directly bearing on V4.

tranche.reason: Tests refusal bypass using injected conversation tokens and demonstration search targeting the first response token, a different method addressing V4.

source_check.notes:
Tables 1/3 report ASRs after three restarts; Tables 7/8 report restart means and standard deviations. The r29/r30 auxiliary notes reverse the mean-result judges.
This is a composite prompt-based V4 test; it does not establish token-position KL concentration or test fine-tuning fragility.
